title: Wave 1 came back: what to land, and 15 decisions the three batches left for you

steps.intro: Each batch is finished on one saved branch per repo. Nothing is landed. I checked that the three do not collide with each other.

steps.path: The chat window, the Office editor's log, background commands
steps.headline: Land the Release safety batch?
steps.today: After a window reload the app opens the oldest chat, so your next message can go to the wrong conversation. The Office editor's error log can copy words from your document. After a restart the assistant is told a background command does not exist.
steps.problem: These three are fixed on a branch, tested in a test copy of the app and reviewed twice. The phone app was not tested; no phone code changed.
steps.proposal: Landing puts all three fixes on master for the 1.4 release. You would notice one thing: after a reload you land on the chat you were on.

options.label: Land it
pros: Reload stops sending messages to the wrong chat.
Document words stay out of bug reports.
The full desktop check passed on the final code.
cons: The Office log now holds less detail for diagnosing editor faults.
Not tried on a phone.

options.label: Hold it
pros: Nothing changes until you have tried it yourself.
cons: The wrong-chat reload stays in the app.
The branch falls behind as other work lands.

steps.path: Developer tools, plus four small app changes
steps.headline: Land the Workspace tools batch?
steps.today: Sessions can lose work in several ways, a push can skip its secrets scan, and an Arch install from the other package downloads 206 MB and then fails to update.
steps.problem: The batch fixes these on a branch (30 changes to the tools, 18 to the app). Its own tests pass, but GitHub's test runs have not run on it and three tools were not tried in real use.
steps.proposal: I would open the pull requests so GitHub runs its tests, and land only if they pass. In the app you would notice: the Arch update message, 'Docs' and 'docs' as two folders on Linux, and a Windows sign-in that retries a refused port.

options.label: Land if tests pass
pros: Pushes cannot skip the secrets scan.
Close-out stops suggesting deleting folders with unsaved work.
Arch users get a clear message instead of a failed download.
cons: Three tools are unproven in real use (test-chat driver, Mac loader, drag test).
143 saved website pictures will differ when next regenerated.

options.label: Land, drop Windows retry
pros: Same as above.
Leaves out the one app change no Windows machine has tried.
cons: Windows sign-in keeps its occasional 'Could not open a local port' failure.

options.label: Hold it
pros: Nothing changes yet.
cons: 48 changes sit on a branch and fall behind.
The next batches would not get the safer push command.

steps.headline: How should the sync impersonation fix go out?
steps.today: A connection signed in to your account can pose as another of your devices and take or release its chat locks.
steps.problem: The fix closes that while a device is connected. Its cost: after a connection drops badly (wifi switch, laptop wake), that device's locks are ignored for up to 45 seconds. In that window a chat can open about 10 seconds slower, a hand-off to it is refused, and the same chat could be opened on two devices. It goes live for every app version minutes after landing.
steps.proposal: A complete fix has each install prove who it is. That needs an app release.

options.label: Ship now, then full fix
pros: Protection starts today.
The 45-second window goes away with the later app release.
cons: Until then you may see a slower chat open after a dropped connection.
Two rounds of change to the same area.

options.label: Ship as built only
pros: Protection starts today.
No further work.
cons: The 45-second window stays for good.
Someone holding your sign-in can still claim an offline device.

options.label: Hold for full fix
pros: No 45-second window ever reaches users.
cons: The gap stays open until an app release.
Nothing improves in the meantime.

steps.path: Games, the Google Messages add-on, theme updates
steps.headline: Land the rest of the Security batch now, or hold Google Messages until tried on Windows?
steps.today: Game result messages have no limit. The Google Messages Windows program carries an old security library. A theme whose files changed without a new version number never shows Update.
steps.problem: All three are fixed and tested, except that the rebuilt Google Messages program has never been run: there is no Windows computer here. It reaches Windows users within about an hour of landing.
steps.proposal: Holding only the Google Messages piece means splitting it off the branch first, a small extra step.

options.label: Land, hold Messages
pros: Games and theme fixes go out now.
No untested program reaches Windows users.
cons: The old security library stays until you or a tester pairs and sends one text on Windows.

options.label: Land everything
pros: The patched library reaches users today.
No splitting needed.
cons: If the rebuilt program fails to start, texting breaks for Windows users until a fix.

options.label: Hold everything
pros: Nothing changes yet.
cons: Game messages stay unlimited.
The branch falls behind.

steps.intro: Found or parked by that batch.

steps.path: Editing a queued message on YouCoded's own engine
steps.headline: Fix the queued-message edit now, or leave it for the chat fixes batch?
steps.today: On YouCoded's own engine, pressing Edit on a waiting message that has a file puts the raw file path in the box and drops the file chip. Claude Code chats are fine.
steps.problem: The retest found it still broken. The batch was told to retest only, so it did not fix it.
steps.proposal: The fix is small (about 25 to 40 lines). Fixing now means it can ship with 1.4.

options.label: Fix it now
pros: Editing a waiting message keeps its file.
Ships with the other release fixes.
cons: One more small change to review before landing.

options.label: Leave for Batch 2
pros: Nothing extra to review now.
cons: The fault stays until the chat fixes batch runs.

steps.path: Chats on a hosted model whose size the app does not know
steps.headline: What size should the app assume for an unknown hosted model?
steps.today: The app assumes such a model can hold 250k. Many hold 128k or less, so long chats fail with a 'too long' error.
steps.problem: A wrong guess either fails (too big) or summarises earlier than needed (too small).
steps.proposal: Lowering to 128k stops failures for the most common hosted size. Models that really are bigger would summarise sooner than they need to. Models of 64k or 32k would still fail.

options.label: Lower to 128k
pros: Fewer 'too long' failures on common hosted models.
cons: Bigger models summarise earlier than necessary.
Smaller models still fail.

options.label: Keep 250k
pros: Big models use their full room.
cons: Long chats keep failing on common hosted models.

steps.path: Three throwaway test chats and one folder-trust entry
steps.headline: Remove the test leftovers the first test round put in your real Claude Code data?
steps.today: The first tester ran the test copy against your real Claude Code data. It left a few tiny chats (named T1-…, T5-s…, Sleep Command Retest) under one scratch project, and a 'trust this folder' entry for that scratch folder.
steps.problem: Test runs are not supposed to write there. The second round used a throwaway home and wrote nothing. This is the fault card #17 describes.
steps.proposal: Removing them deletes only those chats and that one entry. I would do it while your app is closed, or stage it to run after you next quit.

options.label: Remove them
pros: Your chat list has no stray test chats.
cons: Touches your real data folder once, after the app is closed.

options.label: Leave them
pros: Nothing in your data is touched.
cons: The stray chats stay in your past-conversations list.

steps.path: What two of the assistant's own tools say about a command from before a restart
steps.headline: Run the paid evaluation on the changed tool wording?
steps.today: Two of the assistant's tools now report a saved outcome for a background command from before a restart, where they used to say there was none.
steps.problem: A change to what a tool tells the assistant can, rarely, change how models behave. The evaluation measures that and costs money.
steps.proposal: The wording only appears after a restart with a background command, which is rare. A run would need a spending cap from you.

options.label: Skip it
pros: No cost.
The change only shows in a rare case.
cons: A behaviour change on small models would go unmeasured.

options.label: Run with a cap
pros: Measures the effect before release.
cons: Costs money; you set the cap.
Adds a wait before landing.

steps.intro: Decisions that batch wrote onto its cards.

steps.path: What a test copy shares with your real app
steps.headline: Should test copies be private by default?
steps.today: A test copy shares your real sign-ins, Claude Code data and new-session defaults. That is how last night's leftovers got into your real data.
steps.problem: Anything a test does can show up in, or change, your real app.
steps.proposal: Private by default gives each test copy its own empty home. A session that needs your sign-ins (to test a real model, say) would have to ask for 'borrow my sign-ins'.

options.label: Private by default
pros: Tests cannot leave chats or settings in your real app.
Borrowing sign-ins becomes a visible choice.
cons: Some tests need an extra step to reach a real model.
Sessions may ask you for that more often.

options.label: Keep sharing
pros: Tests reach real models with no extra step.
cons: Test leftovers can keep landing in your real data.

steps.path: The unfinished test-speed experiments and pull request #272
steps.headline: Drop the test-speed experiments?
steps.today: Experiments from October tried to make test runs faster. They were never finished. Waits are already down to 5 to 10 minutes from other work.
steps.problem: They keep one old folder and one open pull request alive, and two of their changes exist only on this computer.
steps.proposal: Either way I back up the two unsaved changes first. Dropping closes the pull request and removes the folder.

options.label: Drop them
pros: One less open item and old folder.
The saved copy stays on GitHub if you change your mind.
cons: Any further speed-up would start again from the saved copy.

options.label: Keep them
pros: The work stays ready to pick up.
cons: The folder and pull request keep showing up in every inventory.

steps.path: What must pass before master accepts a change
steps.headline: Require the tests to pass before anything lands on master?
steps.today: Master only requires the Linux build to succeed. The tests run but do not block a landing.
steps.problem: A change with failing tests can land.
steps.proposal: Requiring the tests means every landing waits for them (about 5 to 10 minutes), and an unreliable test can block a landing until it is fixed.

options.label: Require tests
pros: A change that breaks a test cannot land.
Fits your rule that broken tests get fixed at once.
cons: Every landing waits 5 to 10 minutes.
One unreliable test can hold up unrelated work.

options.label: Leave as is
pros: Landings stay quick.
cons: Broken tests can reach master unnoticed.

steps.path: Where the page's source is kept
steps.headline: Where should the Analytics page's source live?
steps.today: The page lives only in your app's Pages folder, with no change history. Sessions back it up by hand.
steps.problem: The workspace repo is public, and the page shows how your usage numbers are gathered.
steps.proposal: A private repo gives it history without publishing it.

options.label: A private repo
pros: History and backups without making it public.
cons: One more repo to keep track of.

options.label: The workspace repo
pros: Everything in one place.
cons: The page's workings become public.

options.label: Leave as is
pros: No change.
cons: Hand backups continue; a bad edit is hard to undo.

steps.path: Three small yes-or-no items from the tools batch
steps.headline: Which of these three small changes do you want? Pick any.
steps.today: Three items wait on you: a check that guards the voice download, a Mac timing fault nobody has reproduced, and unused marketplace settings code.
steps.problem: Each is small but needs your word.
steps.proposal: I recommend all three. None changes what you see in the app.

options.label: Widen voice guard
pros: The voice download check covers more cases.
cons: Slightly more to maintain.

options.label: Drop Mac timing item
pros: Closes an item never reproduced.
cons: If it is real, it would have to be found again.

options.label: Delete unused settings code
pros: Less dead code.
cons: Would be rebuilt if marketplace settings are ever wanted.

steps.path: The four idea pictures on the landing page
steps.headline: Replace the site's idea pictures with the regenerated ones?
steps.today: The site shows four hand-made idea pictures. The release script can now make them itself.
steps.problem: The regenerated paint picture has no brush strokes; the hand-made one did. The four new pictures are in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-destin-youcoded-dev/f75a7970-4f0b-486d-8f97-1e8d03fc1a88/scratchpad/ws4/gallery/
steps.proposal: Your live site is untouched until you choose.

options.label: Fix paint first
pros: The site never shows a blank-looking paint page.
cons: Pictures stay hand-made a little longer.

options.label: Use them now
pros: Pictures refresh themselves on every release.
cons: The paint picture looks emptier than today's.

options.label: Keep hand-made
pros: The look you chose stays.
cons: They go stale as the app changes.

steps.page: Left over from Security and server
steps.intro: Decisions that batch wrote onto its cards.

steps.path: A friend's modified app claiming a forfeit win when you disconnect
steps.headline: Switch the forfeit message off on the server?
steps.today: The server accepts a 'my opponent forfeited' message. No released app sends it, but a modified app can use it to record a win against you.
steps.problem: It is an opening for fake wins and nothing honest uses it.
steps.proposal: Switching it off loses nothing today. The other way is to accept it only when the server saw the match start, which keeps forfeits possible later.

options.label: Switch it off
pros: Fake forfeit wins stop.
Nothing honest is lost.
cons: Real forfeits would need building later if you want them.

options.label: Keep, with a check
pros: Forfeits stay possible for a future app.
cons: More to build and test now for something nobody uses.

steps.path: A phone signed out after 90 days unused
steps.headline: Should the computer tell you when a phone was signed out for being unused?
steps.today: After 90 days unused, a paired phone is signed out. Nothing is shown or recorded on the computer.
steps.problem: You find out only when the phone will not connect.
steps.proposal: A notice would be one quiet line in the remote access settings, not a popup.

options.label: Show a quiet notice
pros: You can see why a phone stopped connecting.
cons: One more line in settings.

options.label: Show nothing
pros: Settings stay as they are.
cons: A dead phone connection stays unexplained.

steps.path: Being signed out when the server rejects a request
steps.headline: Should the app tell you when it signs you out by itself?
steps.today: If the server rejects your sign-in, the app signs you out without saying so.
steps.problem: You notice later, when something that needs your account stops working.
steps.proposal: A notice would say you were signed out and offer Sign in again.

options.label: Show a notice
pros: You know at once and can sign back in.
cons: One more message, in a rare case.

options.label: Show nothing
pros: No new message.
cons: Sign-outs stay silent.

steps.intro: Things every session keeps asking you about.

steps.path: Five folders untouched for two weeks or more
steps.headline: What should happen to the five old work folders every session asks about?
steps.today: Google files, test-speed experiments, helper plans, batcher counters and readme-models are unfinished and unmerged. All three overnight sessions asked you about them.
steps.problem: Four are tied to decisions you have not made yet. The question repeats in every session.
steps.proposal: A keep-list would stop sessions asking about folders you have chosen to keep. That is a small change to a workspace script, so it needs your word.

options.label: Keep all, stop asking
pros: Nothing is lost.
Sessions stop repeating the question.
cons: The folders stay on disk until each decision is made.

options.label: Keep all, keep asking
pros: Nothing is lost, no script change.
cons: Every session keeps asking.

options.label: Remove readme-models only
pros: One folder gone.
cons: Its branch stays saved on GitHub, but the folder would need recreating to continue.

steps.path: Work that exists only on this computer
steps.headline: Back up the two pieces of other sessions' work that exist only on this computer?
steps.today: Your approved sync-conflict deck sits on a branch that is only on this computer. The local engine fixes (#226) are also only here, because the secrets scan flags a line I checked earlier and found is not a real secret.
steps.problem: If this computer's disk failed, both would be gone.
steps.proposal: Yes backs up the deck branch and allows the one scan exception so #226 can be backed up. Neither is landed.

options.label: Back both up
pros: Both are safe on GitHub.
cons: Records one exception in the secrets scanner.

options.label: Deck branch only
pros: The deck is safe.
No scanner exception.
cons: The local engine fixes stay on this computer only.

options.label: Leave both
pros: Nothing changes.
cons: Both stay at risk.
